ing toward socialism say that they have
gained much in this demonstration of
the necessity for a stronger govern
ment control, and the government ownership OF natural monopolies, particu-
larly the railroad companies. Public
attention has been centered upon the
workings OF one trust, and the public has
been compelled to witness a spectacle
of arrogance and greed such as no one
believed possible.

President Roosevelt knows that there
are times when public sentiment is
awake and ready for action, and he be-
lieves that this is one OF those favorable
junctions. Congress will hear from HIM
this winter on the subject of this and
other trusts, and it may be predicted with safety that the matter will
not lie dropped until there have been
results.

From a purely political view point
President Roosevelt's settlement of the
coal strike must be regarded as a very
able move. It was a bold one, whatever
else it was. He was creating precedent.
No man in the White House ever before
has assumed to intervene in an indus-
trial dispute. Cleveland's participation
in the trouble OF 1894 was along the line
of official duty in executing the laws
for preserving order. He did not con-
cern himself with the industrial con-
troversy, and made no attempt to set

Welt did not profess to be acting in his
official capacity, except in so far as his
office enabled him to voice what seem
ed to him demand of the people. But
his action gave an official and definite
expression to an overwhelming public
sentiment, and the people to whom he
spoke were compelled to listen. It was
a case of vox populi with vengeance.
Without the support of public opinion
he could have accomplished nothing. As
it was the public endorsed him unani-
mously, and, in the outcome, the pub
lic is grateful for his services. He might
have shirked. He could have pleaded
lack of authority, and in so doing he
could have earned the everlasting grati-
tude of the coal barons and the J. Pier-
pont Morgans, big and little, all over
the country. But Roosevelt is not the
sinking kind, and nothing could be
more characteristic than this indiffer-
ence to conventionalities. It was noth-
ing to him that no previous president
had ever taken such step. He did not
inquire into the custom or etiquette
applicable to this sort of an occasion.
He looked only for what he believed
was the right and having made himself
sure of that he went ahead. No one
can accuse him of indulging in the
spectacular; it was not sham battle
or "grandstand" play. It was really
a test of power between vested wealth
as represented by Morgan & co. and
on the other hand, public opinion, the
voice of the people who spoke thru the
president of the United States.

It has puzzled a good many to under-
stand how so shrewd, successful, worldly
wise men such as the presidents OF the
coal carrying railroads are supposed TO
be, and undoubtedly are, could do
and say the foolish things and
deliberately court the disapproval of the
public at large, and the inevitable at-
tacks thru state and NATIONAL legis-
latures.

The whole thing will be easier to under-
stand if attention is kept on J. Pier-
pont Morgan. The half dozen railroad
presidents are figures. Morgan
controls the railroads and them. He
has dictated the policy from the begin-
ning. Part OF the time he has chosen
to keep in the background. When there
was any dealing TO take he has been
quite willing to put it up to the railroad
presidents. He has told the public that
he was quite helpless, he would gladly
do something and was even planning to
bring in a ship load of coal from Europe.
He regretted that the railroad presi-
dents were such obstinate gentlemen,
and hinted that he would labor with
them to see the error of their ways.

But when it came to a more agreeable
role—when it came TO the stage of of-
fering arbitration (a certain plausi-
ble sort) and doing something THAT
might lead to a settlement of the strike
then your uncle Pierpont was right to the front. He quite forgot about having
no influence with the coal operators,
and came trooping along IN his private
car (for Baer's) and had a nice
public chat with the president. There
was hardly a pretense OF keeping up
the fiction that the coal load presidents
were the real people, and he only a
sympathetic onlooker.

Keene, all powers in the financial world, it is thought that as soon as they arrive here, they will shake UP things in the stock market. WHAT'S more, the business conditions warrant these advances, and good and growing business will keep the prices high for months or years after they reach the high water mark.

Stock Of the St. Paul Road.

The Commercial Advertiser has a chapter on the annual report of the Chicago Milwaukee, St. Paul railway company. After giving the statistics already published the paper says: The report of the company for the year ending June, 1901, showed net earnings applicable to dividends on the stock of about 8 per cent. During the past year the funded debt and fixed charges have been reduced by the conversion of bonds into capital stock, so that it is reported that the capital stock is now about $103,900,000. Last year the fixed charges were $6,383,900; which is probably reduced to about $6,600,000. If the miscellaneous income remains constant, the net earnings applicable to dividends will be about $8,400,000, which is 8 1 per cent on the estimated outstanding capital stock of $103,900,000. St. Paul's charges for maintenance have been rather high for a number of years, so we can safely add 1,900,000 to the reported earnings to arrive at the actual earning capacity of the property, which will thus be seen to be something over 10 per cent on the capital stock.

At first glance it would naturally be assumed that so large an increase in earnings as shown by St. Paul, especially when this is combined with reduction in fixed charges, would tend to increase the rate of earnings on the common stock. But the conversion of the bonds into common stock in this instance is an exception to the general rule that a decrease in fixed charges works to the advantage of the dividend rate on the stock. The bonds which are being converted are being exchanged, because it is to the advantage of the bondholders to do so, whereas, ordinary refundings are put in operation because of the benefits which will accrue to the stockholders of the corporation. The bonds which are being exchanged were issued many years ago, and at that time the St. Paul company had not developed as large earnings for its stock as are being shown at the present time, so the increased rate of earnings for the stock is due to the great earning power of the property and not on account of the reduction in fixed charges.

The operating department of the St. Paul company has been very conservative and slow to adopt new methods of operation. It has retained its old locomotives and cars and heavier equipment has been supplied only when the demands of increased traffic made the increase absolutely necessary. In this respect the road has a large reserve up its sleeve. If gross earnings should fall off, the company could, by means of economies now practiced on most of the larger systems, reduce its operating expenses particularly by increasing its train load. With the excellent showing as indicated by the figures reported with the possibilities of reduced operating expenses as mentioned, with the great financial and material development of the territory that it serves, there is no question but that the St. Paul is in position to maintain continuously a high rate of dividends.

For the Chief Executive of the Nation never hunts in Colorado beating up or down its mountain streams or winding in and out along its tortuous mountain paths, without the services of John Goff as guide and companion.

John Goff is a resident of Crawfordsville. At least when he speaks of home in that fashion peculiar to those men who have gone into the wilderness of the West, he refers to the little cottage nestled away among the sycamore trees that line a lonesome, half neglected byway of the old Hoosier town.

Goff spent his boyhood days near Ladoga, a little village scarcely half dozen miles away from Crawfordsville. Here there are half hundred people inhabiting the countryside. We yet remember the sturdy young man when he fished in Indiana streams and beat through Indiana woods in search of game. His father and his grandfather were trappers before him, his uncles and his great-uncles were hunters, and his mother had in her veins the restless blood of the pioneers wife. In John Goff the traits of the family centred.

That is one of the reasons he is selected annually to be the companion and the guide of President Roosevelt. For Theodore Roosevelt, hunter, like the men of his kind, loves a man after his own heart.

Goff at the age of fifteen had already brought his name prominently before the people of his own neighborhood. He had on this occasion been sent by his father to the home of a friend. His journey, however, was delayed until darkness had begun to fall, and young Goff, when finally he did put out, found it necessary to make his way through the woods, where already the darkness had grown dense.

ficulty.

marked his extraordinary career.

to interfere with business. Among
his associates in the city he never
mentioned them, nor did he permit
lAem to be mentioned to him Up to
the last Mr.. Rhodes kept firm grip
on all those vast South African inter.
ests created and controlled by him.
Except that he was more irritable and
more dictatorial there was no outward
change in his method Of handling men,
millions and empires.

The Dresdner Journal of yesterday says: "The princess, in a state of intense mental excitement, suddenly deserted her family at Salzburg and went abroad. The Saxon court functions for the winter, including the New Year's reception, have been cancelled."

The foregoing paragraph in yesterday's official journal, which was inserted by order of the king and crown prince of Saxony, has turned into truth what for several days past has been regarded as an incredible tale. The crown princess of Saxony, surrounded by her ladies-in-waiting and numerous attendants and servants of the royal household, has vanished so utterly that the police of every kingdom of Europe have for ten days been unable to trace her. The official announcement was made in order to obtain the aid of the general public in finding the princess, and because the court fiction that she preferred to remain in retirement at Salzburg rather than to return to her husband and children at Dresden can no longer be maintained.

A week after their arrival at the castle the prince broke his leg while hunting and was brought back to Dresden. The princess, however, remained at the castle. Why she did so the people of the court did not know, except that, with gloomy tenacity, the princess usually does what she pleases.

Spray, with Col. Gaynor and Capt. Green

nor and Capt. Green to stay at the Wind

gan, when application would be made for
their release on bail.

consultation with Detective Carpenter and

should keep in seclusion until the prisoners

This will give both sides an opportunity

the next sitting of the court."

brace an exhaustive discussion of the va-
rious questions of taxation raised in the
hearing of the case.


The mandamus case of the state com-
missioner of labor against the tax asses-
sors of Lancaster county, which was brought
to test the validity of the law requiring
assessors to gather information for the
State Bureau of Labor and Industrial Stat-
istics, will be argued and submitted to the
supreme court next week. The act in ques-
tion was passed by the legislature of 1897,
but has never been enforced. Each year
since the passage some of the counties
have failed to make the returns required
and as a result the statistics put forth by
the department have been incomplete and
oftentimes misleading. The fusion authori-
ties gave notice several times that man-
damus proceedings would be commenced, if
necessary, but the bluff was never made
good.


Confident Law Will Hold.


"I am confident the law will stand the
test," said Deputy Labor Commissioner
Watson today, "but it has been so generally
questioned and violated that the only way
to determine its worth is by the mandamus
process. The state spends a lot of money
each year publishing reports of statistics
gathered under the act. They are incom-
plete and therefore of little value. If the
reports are not correct there is no reason
why they should be printed. If the court
sustains the law we will force the county
assessors to do the work. We have to
begin mandamus proceedings against every-
one of them."

perior quality, a law similar to the Ne-
braska act is in force. Several days ago

views at your convenience."

WASHINGTON, D. C., April 7.—The Cuban reciprocity question will come up in the House tomorrow, when the Payne bill, providing for a 20 per cent. reduction of the tariff on all Cuban products is to receive the consideration of the lower branch of Congress. Whether or not the bitter and notable struggle that went on in the ranks of the Republican party over this question, a few weeks ago, will be revived during the consideration of the bill by the whole House remains to be seen. Just now it seems doubtful, because the ranks of the opposition Republicans have been greatly reduced since that time by the wonderful missionary work of the leaders of the dominant party, but something may happen during the course of debate to fan into flame the smouldering fire of discomfort among the opponents of reduction, and if this happens something lively may be looked for.

Already the leaders of the opposition have announced their intention to keep out of the fight for fear their remarks against the proposed reduction may be used by the Democrats as campaign material. A number of Republicans will, however, speak against the measure.

The Democrats are, as usual, divided. The large majority, however, favor absolute free trade with Cuba, and will watch every opportunity during the debate to open up the whole tariff question. All Democrats interested in sugar—principally the Louisianians and those from the best sugar districts—will fight any reduction. In the Senate the Democrats will fight with the unity and bulldog determination they showed in regard to the Tillman-McLaurin affair, and it is probable that the party in the House to put forward a solid front also.

The 20 per cent proposition will probably carry in the end, although the rebate scheme, which provides for the payment by the United States of a rebate to the Cuban Government, to be paid over to the Cuban planters to reimburse them for the duty charged on their sugar, has some strong supporters.

CAMPAIGN MATERIAL.

At all events it is up to the Democrats to get some campaign material out of the fight and they are making every preparation to do so. The fight will probably last for three or four days in the House.

Representative Lassiter has been working upon the officials of the War Department for some time in the interest of William D. Smith, late private Troop H., U. S. Cavalry, who is at present in prison at Leavenworth, having allowed two Philippine prisoners to escape some months ago, and this morning his efforts were rewarded by the receipt of a letter from the Judge advocate general saying that he had been informed by the Assistant Secretary of War that Smith's penalty would be reduced to an imprisonment of six months.

Smith is from Petersburg, and has a most excellent record. He has been in the army for nine years and before going to the Philippines he had seen service in the West and in Cuba. The charges against him are that he was guilty of negligence, but no intentional breach of his duty as a soldier. Smith's aged mother is now living in Petersburg, and it is on her account entirely that Mr. Lassiter has worked so hard to save the prisoner. The Congressman from the Fourth expressed himself to-day as extremely gratified at the success of his efforts.

By the time the orders in the case are issued Smith's six months will have expired and he will be ordered to proceed to San Francisco upon the first transport that sails for the States. eating. To attract his attention one of

end of the fallen trees and tried to
teeter. The bear, half rising, turned his

snoring. This is an absolutely true

cholera has satisfied the American au-
thorities that only the most rigorous

building which is unsanitary must
come down and be removed, the low
places in the city are to be filled in,
suitable sewerage is to be insisted on,
walls are to be built to hold back tide
water and new buildings Will be per-
mitted only in compliance with strict
regulations as to plumbing and con-
struction which will insure healthful
conditions.


1t is estimated that when the build

be moved out into temporary camps.

looked after in their temporary quar-

gives it as his opinion that it will be
necessary to fill in over the whole site
of the city in order to secure the
grades that will make it possible to
drain the streets and houses and ac-
complish safe sanitary conditions.

that the reclamation of the San Nicolas
beach will cost at least 100000.

Washington, May. Cerebral hemorrhage was the immediate cause of Rear Admiral W. T. Sampson's death.

The rear admiral had been in a semi-conscious state for several days and yesterday forenoon suffered a severe cerebral hemorrhage. At the bedside when the rear admiral breathed his last were Mrs. Sampson, Mrs. Cluverius, the rear admiral's married daughter; two young sons, Ralph and Harold Sampson; Dr. Dixon, the attending physician; and nurses and attendants.

Mrs. Sampson has broken down under the severe strain, and was quite ill all during the day. But for the critical condition of her husband she would have been confined to her bed.

While no definite arrangements have as yet been made concerning the funeral ceremonies, it is probable they will take place on Thursday at the Church of the Covenant in this city. The remains will be taken to the rear admiral's old home at Palmyra, N. Y. for interment.

William T. Sampson was born in Palmyra, Wayne county, New York, on Feb. 5, 1810. Up to the time of the outbreak of the war with Spain he was comparatively unknown outside of naval circles, and up in Wayne county, where he visited often, everybody knew him as Billy Sampson. His father was a day laborer, and as a boy and youth William often accompanied his father to places near the Sampson home, where he helped at "odd jobs."

Young Sampson found time to attend school in an irregular way, and showed so much ambition that he attracted the attention of William H. Southwick, of Palmyra, who spoke of him to E. B. Morgan, at that time representing the district in congress, and the lad received through Morgan his appointment as naval cadet at Annapolis. His record at the academy was good, and when his class was graduated, about a year before the beginning of the civil war, the name of William T. Sampson stood first on the list.

Sampson first won fame and recognition on the old "Patapsco" when he formed part of the blockading squadron at Charleston in 1861. The harbor had been mined by the confederates, and when the blockading Admiral decided to enter the harbor he detailed the Patapsco to go ahead and clear the area.

Sampson was executive officer of the ironclad, and as the vessel steamed into the harbor he stood on the bridge in the most exposed position on the boat. He was a fascinating mark for the sharpshooters. As the little boat entered the harbor bullets from their rifles rained upon it. Sampson's men fell all around him, struck by the leaden missiles. He ordered them below and faced the fire alone. Slowly and carefully the mine-destroyer went ahead on its hunt.

Suddenly there was an ominous roar, columns of water were thrown into the air, and mingled with the liquid streams were the guns, turrets and sheathing of the gallant boat. Of the crew twenty-five were saved by other boats from the fleet; seventy-five sank in Charleston harbor. Sampson was blown 100 feet in the air and fell in the water many feet from where his boat went down. He was as calm when picked up as though he had been for a swim in the brooks of Wayne county and was on deck ready for business on the following day.

After the breaking out of the war Sampson blockaded the ports of Cuba with his squadron, being joined in this work by the flying squadron under Rear Admiral Schley, who was next in command to him. At the time of the fight off Santiago, on July 8, 1898 Sampson, with his flagship, had started for Siboney, giving the signal, "Disregard the movements of the flagship," but returned after the battle was over.

The details of the controversy in regard to the credit for the destruction of the Spanish warships are fresh in the public mind.

Rear Admiral Sampson was married twice. His first wife was Margaret Aldrich, a niece of Pliny T. Sexton, of Palmyra, N. Y. They were married in 1862 and had five daughters, four of whom are living.

Rear Admiral Sampson's second wife was Miss Elizabeth Burling, who went to Palmyra from Canandaigua as a teacher in one of the schools. By this marriage Rear Admiral Sampson had two sons, Ralph and Harold.

Not the red fires of Vulcan,
Nor Cyclops' pristine powers.
Could match their feats of magic
Who shape this world of ours!
With myriad painting engines.
With countless picks and drills,
They arch the threatening rivers,
They pierce the hostile hills:
In steam and smoke and lightning


Earth's captive forces play,
To weld with Titan touches
The city of to-day.
Still from their sunken footholds


Those cobweb buildings rise,
Whose panes ray back the morning,


Whose foreheads touch the skies;
While many crowded workshop,


And toiling mill and mine,
Yields up its costly treasures


To make them fair and fine.
Yet. void of civic honor,


OF justice, light and law,
What were the proudest structures


That e'er the round world saw?
Rome was a queenly empire,

And fame and triumphs failed her,


With sons no longer great.

Her fortunes wax apace.
While Virtue guards her nearthstones,

That dwarf the courts of kings
A free and glorious city


or incorporeal things

"I was standing on the stoop," said the policeman.

"Were they disorderly?" interrupted the magistrate.

The policeman insisted upon telling the story in his own way so the prisoners were discharged.

Breeders IN this State Lose Thousands Annually By Ticks.

Since The stock law went into effect, and ticks have disappeared in many parts OF the State, Texas fever has become a common disease. It is estimated that the breeders OF the State are now losing annually more than $4,000 from this disease, and it has been shown to be so important that the South Carolina experiment station has undertaken the work OF combating its ravages by process OF inoculation (vaccination).

In the fall OF 1900 twelve calves were bought by the veterinary division, of which Dr. G. T. Nesom is chief and Dr. Shealey assistant. All OF them were subject to the disease, as they had never carried ticks. They were inoculated with blood from a cow that was immune, and in a few days they developed light cases OF the disease from which they soon recovered. During the summer OF 1891 they were kept in tick-infested pasture and many of them contracted the mild form Of the disease.

But more important work is now being done in the same way on Northern cattle. Every one who has purchased cattle from the North and exposed them to the Southern cattle tick knows that most of them die the first year OF "acclimation fever," another name for Texas fever.

Since 100 head OF beef cattle were brought down from Indianapolis in November, 1901, and have been inoculated, they are doing well so far and when the work is finished in the Spring they will be tested in tick-infested pastures. It is hoped they will prove immune. If this method proves entirely successful it will establish the fact that a great obstacle in the way of introducing better cattle into this State has been removed.

In this Connection Dr. G. T. Nesom has sent out the following circular letter to farmers and cattle raisers in South Carolina.

This circular letter is sent you in order to assist the veterinarians in securing the cattle against Texas fever.

During the past few years the disease has been prevalent in many sections of the State, but since the passage of the present stock law it has been found in the counties and in the pastures and pens OF stock buyers and feeders. Texas fever is known by a number OF names, but the most important OF these are Splenic fever, Splenetic fever, acclimation fever, Southern cattle fever, tick fever, red water, bloody murrain, bloody urine, distemper, mountain distemper and many local names.

The symptoms are readily recognized by any one who has seen cattle suffering from this fever. At first the animals become stupid and leave the herd for some secluded and shady part of the pasture. They appear listless and droop, as if all energy had forsaken them, the ears drop, the nose is more or less dry, rumination (chewing cud) suspended, the urine light to dark red in color, and constipation marked, only small quantities of very dark, dry dung being voided. They are highly fevered, the temperature running from 103 to 107 degrees F. In milk cows the flow OF milk is almost suspended. All OF the symptoms increase in severity until the animal becomes almost or quite unconscious, walks round in circles, groans and seems to suffer real pain. Then convulsions set in, the animal falls, unconscious and snoring in the intervals between convulsions, until death ensues. Calves rarely develop the severe symptoms or die from the disease, but in cattle over year old the death rate is possibly 30 to 90 per cent, increasing as the age increases.

Post mortem examination of the carcass shows the flesh to be almost bloodless and pale in color, the spleen enlarged, black and easily torn, the bladder filled with bloody urine, the liver and intestines yellowish and the gall bladder filled with bile.

A thorough examination of the skin about the thighs, flanks, neck and other parts OF the body reveals the presence OF ticks, which always go with Texas fever. The cause OF the disease is a small animal organism, protozoan, which seems at all times to exist in the body of the tick. When the tick inserts its bite through the hide these little germs gain access to the blood of the cow and there develop, producing cases of Texas fever in ten to twenty days. Death results from the destruction OF the red blood cells, the refuse going to the spleen and the coloring matter to the bladder.

Cattle that have had ticks on them when they were calves are immune TO the disease and will not have it again. Cattle that have not had ticks on them until year old, will develop the disease as soon as they get the ticks.

The experiment station officials desire to assist the stockmen OF the State in getting the disease under control and prevent severe losses in future. Inoculation experiments are now in progress, and it is hoped that immunity to it may be produced by artificial means.

You are requested to answer the questions on the enclosed postal card and return as soon as possible to the veterinarian, who wishes to thank you in advance for your cooperation in the matter. Yours truly,

G. T. Nesom, Veterinarian.

Fields store, Texas. Dear Happyhammers: I have been quite a while since last wrote to our dear old Happy page, I suppose I am almost forgotten to Happyhammers. To tell you in plain, honest words, the reason of my negligence is I have been financially enharassed. But as soon as I recovered the very first thing I thought of was the Happy page and how I had neglected my correspondence with it, so in good cheer once more take the pleasure of being with the Happyhammers for a few moments.

Vacation is over and we gather up our books to begin school for another long season. I am glad of it, though for different reasons. I like almost every other country boy, like to stop work and start to school and store up knowledge for future use. I am always ready to stop work, you know. And then I suppose that little boys and all were growing tired of so much warm weather and all welcome autumn with her falling leaves and cool nights, barns full of corn and hay and sweet potatoes half as large as your head. I like School Girl's idea of a boy, and wish I could act as she says, too. I read her letter, and that was she told all of the boys' faults (and a heap more too) and never even mentioned one of the girls' faults. Now isn't that just like a girl? They can sit and write or talk for hours at a time of boys' misdoings, and tell what Brother John did that he ought not to have done, but girls' faults are kept perfectly quiet. Of course, as a general rule boys are not near as good looking or as elegant, or as good about almost ANYTHING, but they don't like to be told or I think boys ought not to be pecked so much. Who is it that harnesses the horse, who milks ten cows in an old muddy pen, who runs and does this, that and the other? The boy in almost all instances. I don't think the girls of our club have any right to fuss at the boys, do you, Happy? Some of the members write about Whist biscuits they can make. You just ought to see my biscuits, they are simply fine. Last January mother and the girls were all sick at once, and, of course, the cooking naturally went very well, but biscuits just didn't get right. Once I asked mother's advice regarding the construction of the biscuits. She said to make them with buttermilk and soda and lard, so I put 4 cookspoonfuls of soda and a bit of lard to every four biscuits and made two at once. But after a while I got impatient and worked them all together so they would all be alike. In a half hour's time we had the most ungraceful biscuits you ever saw. Everything looked ugly even Roosevelt (that is what I named the dish, because it was such a popular during the campaign). And of all the biscuits! I can make no attempt to describe them, for you all would think I was exaggerating.

Have any of you taken notice of how many disasters have befallen the world this year? I believe there have been twice as many catastrophes this year as any previous year since I can remember. In nearly every Post Times we read the account of some sad difference, and ninety-two of them are in the South. And you will notice, nearly all the disasters fall on some large city. I am getting very afraid for Fields store.

Mrs. Foster have won decided what our next contest will be. Our last debate was a very interesting one, but I don't agree with the Happy's decision that Washington was greater than Columbus. I remain, as ever, your friend, William Yaught.

shire, Texas. Dear Happyhammers: I thought I would step in and chat with you. I had thunder last night and it is not as hot as it was when last I wrote to the page. My last letter was not printed; and I have no one to blame but my own careless self. For mamma and I went to spend Sunday at Uncle Josh and Aunt Josie's. I ought to have gone to Sunday school, but Uncle Josh made me cry and called me baby. When mamma came you ought to have seen him! He threw his arms around me and said he was teasing you and made you cry. Just tell her you stumbled your toe and I will buy you nickel's worth of candy.

I told mamma I stumbled my toe. Mamma don't think it is right to tease little folks, especially about the boys, as he was teasing me to tell stories. But when I got home, I told mamma I would tell her something that I had done, but it was wrong—that I would give her some candy if she would not whip me. She said she didn't want the candy, but for me, tell her and she would promise not to whip me. Then I told her I had told her a story over at Uncle Josh's for he gave me some candy and I would not do so any more. She said I had acted a lady, and told her about it, and I was glad to help mamma all I can. I wash dishes, dust, sweep, and home times she lets me iron handkerchiefs when I am at home. I am going to school now as I intend to study hard this session. I am not going to be the little boy in Sunday.

I thought the problems of the evolutionary controversy were evidently stirring in his mind when in 1872 he published "Erewhon or Over the Range," a work which comes nearest to Gulliver's Travels in mordant irony and startling paradox of all that has been written in that vein since the death of Swift. Up to now Sir Butler had done nothing to win a reputation, though fourteen years earlier he had passed with some distinction through St. John's College, Cambridge, like his grandfather and father. "Erewhon"—of course, the inverted form of "nowhere"—is an imaginary country, the scene of a fantastic Utopian romance, which is the vehicle for satire aimed at many of the institutions and the ideas of modern society. The ironic humor is rarely as savage as Swift's and is somewhat erratic in its strokes. But the striking and picturesque narration, not too closely bound by systematic theory, enables the reader to realize a topsy-turvy world, in which most things are unlike our own, though human nature subsists under strange civilization and surroundings. The Erewhonians punish disease as a crime, and subject moral offences to quasi-medical treatment, and the main principle of their polity is to exclude by penalties the production of machinery. In the end the traveller who tells the tale escapes by stratagem in a balloon, and leaves behind him a record of a miracle which becomes the basis of an elaborately superstitious creed. In continuation published only last year, "Erewhon Revisited," Mr. Butler records how in a second visit the vanished adventurer skated the mythical system, of which he had become the central figure. The story is more coherent, the irony more trenchant, and the satire of a graver severity. It is a substantially vehement attack on supernatural religion. Mr. Butler was a very Broad Church man, indeed. In another work, "Fair Haven," he drew a painfully satirical picture of religious narrowness, which was deceptive, we believe, by many of the objects of his sarcasm—grave and earnest indeed.

The love of paradox which inspired these ironic studies carried with him in his excursions into the region of classical scholarship. His prose translations of the "Iliad" and the Odyssey were somewhat harsh and cramped in style, but they testified to his close acquaintance with the text of Homer. In his book, "The Authoress of the Odyssey," he evolved some amazing theories about the authorship of the Homeric poems. He thought the Odyssey written by a woman. He held that the name Homer meant hostage, and that the "Iliad" was composed by an actual hostage in the hands of the Greeks, who had his reasons for hating both sides, and who deliberately told the tale of Troy in such a fashion as to hold up Achilles and the other victorious heroes to odium and ridicule. It is probable that Mr. Butler started this theory as a hoax, but there can be little doubt that he wrote himself into the acceptance of it, in the end, with complete and genuine conviction.

It is not very widely known that Mr. Butler was not only a keen musician, but a composer in the style of Handel, of whom he was an ardent admirer. He published, in collaboration with Mr. H. F. Jones, an opera, "Narcissus," in which some musical critics held that the Handelian methods were executed with astonishing skill. His interest in painting and architecture was also keen, and rested upon a thorough knowledge, in especial, of the art history of parts of North Italy. His books "Alps and Sanctuaries" and "Ex Voto," in the latter of which he rescued from oblivion the artistic fame of Tabachetti, the sculptor of the images in the chapels at Varallo, were a revelation to many. But here again, he showed his independence by unsparing severity in his criticism of Raphael's school.

On being brought back to London he was placed in a nursing home, and appeared to be recovering; but his strength had ebbed too far. H., July 20 (Special).—A rather depressing week of almost continuous rain has not been to the advantage of White Mountain resorts, and among the smaller hotels there is regret that the fine prospect of the early season has suffered from bad weather conditions. Instead there are now fine bands of skilled musicians under the best direction obtainable. The season among theatrical companies makes available in summer the rank and file of theatre orchestras from all the cities, and careful selection and the most finished concert work is uniformly required in the interest of a public patronage which has grown critical to degree.

Play over the Waumbek links for the Raymond Cup has been feature of White Mountain golf this week. Only contestants forty-nine years of age and older have been eligible, and guests of the Mount Pleasant House, Crawford House, Profile House, Wentworth Hall and the Intervale House have competed. The cup is a handsome prize offered by Charles L. Raymond, of Chicago, and the man making the lowest gross over eighteen holes at previously stated time of play before July 31 wins the trophy.

The combined orchestras of the Mount Pleasant House and the Mount Washington House, including twenty-five pieces which giving daily concerts at the former, previous the opening of the latter, furnish musical treat rarely enjoyed at any resort hotel. Baldwin, was the moving spirit in a recent minstrel show, and acquitted himself as creditably in former years.

Eight local brokerage firms are involved in the suspension yesterday C. Seymour & Co., the New York brokerage firm. It is feared that some of these concerns will be forced to suspend and that their customers will be heavy losers unless something can be secured from the New York concern, which does not at present seem likely.

The following local houses had Seymour & Co. correspondents: J. D. Fowler & Co., of 1921 F Street; Stitt & Co. of 1881 T; Charles Scott; Schroeder & Co., 705 Seventh Street; J. N. Longshaw, in the LeDroit Building and Corcoran Building; Ernest Humphrey & Co., 1928 F. and Simpson & Jenkins.

The sums lost by the various houses vary, but are said to average about $1,000 each. In a number of cases the concerns had no other connections in New York except Seymour & Co. and are now out of business, temporarily at least, with no wire connections and no money. The more important of the firms, however, had other correspondents, and have continued in business with them.

J. D. Fowler & Co. state that their loss is about 100. J. N. Fowler said to a reporter of The Times this afternoon that he had personally settled the losses in his firm with its customers, and that there would be no suspension, and no loss to customers. He expressed the belief that he would secure settlement with Seymour & Co. in some form, and would not lose by the failure. Fowler & Co. have another correspondent in New York.

Another of the heaviest losers by the failure was the firm of Ernest Humphrey & Co. Mr. John Humphrey, a brother of the senior member of the firm, stated this afternoon that his house had lost about $4,000. Ernest Humphrey became suspicious of the stability of Seymour & Co. last Saturday and went to New York where he has been since that time looking after the interests of his firm.

Last week, Mr. John Humphrey said, Seymour & Co. did not make settlement one night, and we became suspicious. We wired to the firm and insisted on a remittance. They sent over $1,000, and for once this quieted our fears. On Saturday, however, they failed to make a remittance again, and my brother went to New York. He immediately notified the house that he would secure a warrant if our balance was not forthcoming.

They gave him a check on Sunday and it was presented at the opening of the bank the next morning. It was pronounced no good. Since then he has been making every effort to secure a settlement and he tells me that he expects to secure settlement in full.

Humphreys & Co. have another correspondent, Dresser Smith & Co., who have offices in the Maritime Building in New York. They have not suspended, but those of their customers who had business with the Seymour wire will have to wait for a few days for a settlement, Mr. Humphreys says.

King & Co. were perhaps the largest losers by the failure. The firm was composed of Capt. T. H. King andiente Jacobs. They had two offices, one in the Atlantic Building, and another in 559 F Street. The offices have each been doing large business, and the loss will be considerable, if they fail upon a large number of customers if a settlement is not reached with Seymour & Co.

Captain King has just returned from New York. He said to a Times reporter this afternoon that he had employed lawyers in New York to look after his interests.

He has suspended temporarily on account of the Seymour affair, but he is confident that he will be able to resume business at an early day.

Stitt & Co., who were reported to have lost $10,000, really only lost a little, over $500. Mr. David J. Crockett, the silent partner of the firm, paid in his customers in full today and the firm is still doing business. They also have the Dresser, Smith & Co. wire.

Scott & Co. did not lose much, so it is said. They are still doing business to-day. Frank Barnard, who was the Washington representative of Schroeder Co., located at 705 Seventh Street, is another loser by the failure. The loss, however, will not seriously embarrass them, and the offices are still open to business.

J. N. Longshaw, having offices in the LeDroit Building and the Corcoran Building, is another sufferer. The total losses in Washington due to the failure will probably amount to $26,600. Much of this, it is believed, will be recovered. The understanding is that Seymour & Co. have some substantial assets that can be realized upon. While the failure has been widespread, it has not been disastrous. King & Co. was the only firm to suspend entirely.

At a special feature for the entertainment of the thousands who will visit St. Marys during the eighth annual convention and tournament of the Northwestern Volunteer Firemen's Association on August 13, 14 and 15, the committee having the affair in charge have secured the famous Repasz band of Williamsport, to present on the evening of Thursday, August 14, at the driving park, the grand spectacular military concert "The Spanish War."

The production is a tone picture of the recent conflict between the United States and Spain, and the services of over 800 people are required. A grand chorus of over one hundred mixed voices add much to the musical effect of the program, and the band soloists discourse sweet melodies during the progress of the concert.

To give the audience a more vivid idea of the battles as they occurred on land and sea an immense projector-scope, or moving picture machine, is used to throw the views on canvas directly over the stage. In order that the audience may more closely follow the movements of the troops as they portray the various charges an immense search-light is used to bring them into view. The park is lighted as bright as day with arc and incandescent lights.

The program is divided into four parts. The first presents the nation's prosperity, during which the Inauguration of President McKinley takes place, followed by the mutterings of strife, and then the blowing up of the Maine in the harbor of Havana. The second part presents the troops at the front after the late President's call for 125,000 volunteers.

Part three is probably the most realistic, presenting as it does the great battlefield scene. During this part vocal numbers are featured. Mr. S. X. Lent was a delegate from the farmers of Allegan Co., Michigan, to Western Canada to report on the prospects for new settlement. His report is as follows:

I went from Winnipeg to Edmonton, thence east one hundred miles by wagon. I found the country in the vicinity a rich, black loam, from 11 inches to 3 feet deep. The crops are simply something enormous. Wheat and oats by actual measurement often standing FIVE feet high. I have been a farmer for forty years and consider myself a judge in the yield of grain, and I saw wheat that would yield 50 bushels now, and oats that would yield 100 bushels per acre; not one alone, but many. As for root crops and truck, in no country have I ever found their equal for all kinds except potatoes and tomatoes, the nights being long enough for these to ripen well. As a country it has no equal. East of Edmonton, on the head waters of the Vermillion River, I saw hay meadows containing from 10 to 100 acres of grass standing 4 feet high, and often cutting 3 to 4 tons to the acre. From Edmonton I passed through some fine locations, namely, Maskwacis, Lacombe and other points.

From McLeod I went to Red Deer, thence to Prince Albert, 247 miles north of the main line. For the first fifty miles is fine farming country, the next hundred miles is more stock country. Then at Sask, Rosthern and Duck Lake I found very fine farming country, so that I found a party of Americans from Minnesota buying land for themselves—one party buying 40 acres and the other 90 sections of land for themselves, which they propose to improve at once.

I have travelled over twenty different States and Territories in the Union, and never in my lifetime have I ever seen such magnificent crops, especially as fine a stock country.

Rebuilding the walls is work for men with far away horizons. The oldest part of the building, using a quantity of old hand-split laths, such as we made in the early days of America, and used in the mud houses when it was first erected in 1892. Chicago Chronicle.

 Rev. MacArthur, pastor of the Cavalry Baptist Church, New York, is evidently the optimistic man of the century.

Winsor came home Monday morning from Big Stone Lake from a fishing expedition lasting about two weeks, and the gentlemen report having had a most enjoyable time. After The Times went to press on Monday afternoon Henry H. Rose presented the following communication to the St. Clair county canvassing board:

Port Huron, Mich., Nov. 31, 1902,
To the Board of Canvassers of St. Clair County

Gentlemen—The recount has progressed far enough to satisfy me, beyond all reasonable doubt, that a majority of the votes for St. Clair county were cast for Wesley Davidson for sheriff; and being so satisfied I do not feel that any further expense should be incurred in the matter.

I therefore request that the recount be declared off and the majority of the votes be declared for Wesley Davidson and that certificate of election be issued to him in compliance with the law.

Sincerely yours,

HENRY H. ROSE

The board had counted during the afternoon the townships of Clay and Kenockee. Mr. Rose gained in one township and lost in another.

When Mr. Rose asked the board to stop counting the ballots of the county Wesley Davidson was ahead. The board is in session today checking the returns, and making footings. Certificates of election will be issued during the day and it is expected the board will adjourn this evening.

After Mr. Rose's communication was received the canvassing board notified all of the election inspectors brought to Port Huron that they could take their boxes home with them.—Port Huron Daily Times, Nov. 2.

The county board of canvassers met at the county clerk's office Wednesday forenoon, made the proper footings, signed certificates of election, and adjourned sine die. It was decided to place the majority of Wesley Davidson, Democratic candidate for Sheriff, at 15, 10 more than the inspectors' reports showed.

A youthful friend of mine, with the aid of her seamstress, lately completed a love of a frock of this kind. The design, she tells me, was copied from one recently sold in a smart shop on the Avenue de l'Opera. So far as I could observe, the gown displayed no striking innovations in style, although it carefully followed all the present requirements. The neck and shoulders were covered with fine pleated swiss and lace yoke that fell well below the bust line. The swiss and lace formed epaulets while bands of narrow satin ribbon lined the shoulders and formed applied knots on the sleeves. A ribbon flower clasped at the waist, also making the indentations of the band on the front of the decolletage. The sleeves below the epaulets were quite simple, for the organdie fell in full, loose drapery to a pleated and ribbon trimmed cuff at the wrist. At the elbow a band of ribbon tied around the arm divided the sleeve into two skillfully adjusted balloon-shaped draperies.


Scant and Deep.


Although only two flounces, moderately deep and scant, trimmed the skirt, these were so elegantly overlaid with satin ribbon that they gave the impression of being part of a quite elaborate decoration. The upper flounce was indented along its upper border and headed with two rows of the satin, tiny bows appearing at each of the points. Furthermore, double lines of the ribbon finished off the lower part of each. A bow and streamers of the ribbon were suspended from the rear of the girdle and fluttered down the back of the skirt.


A deep, full yoke was particularly graceful, and apropos of it, sheer white swiss pleated, shirred, hand-stitched and subdivided by insertions of lace or embroidery or inset with lace motifs may be had in the shops ready for use. No seamstress, however great her accomplishments, can hope to rival the machine-finished fabrics. These pretty accessories of the wash toilet make up liric sleeves, bloused fronts and sometimes even entire waists to be worn with separate skirts. Some of the fabrics are open spaces through which wash ribbon may be threaded. Considering the variety of uses to which these fabrics may be put, there is no excuse for lack of individuality even in the simple summer gown.


Another lesson which suggested itself to me in studying my fair friend's costume was that a very sensible way had been found for making up wash sleeves. Elaborate ones usually issue from the laundry shorn of their first glory. Her sleeves, when the ribbon tackled about the elbow is removed, are straight and smooth and even the most inexpert laundress can manage them to advantage. It occurred to me that these sleeves would be even prettier if two ribbons were used instead of one, for then they could be divided into three puffs instead of into two.


Shirt Waist Suits

The two bands of dark blue bordered both sides of the open jacket and almost covered the basqued portion, which was narrow and rounded in front. The wide bell-shaped sleeves were filled in with muslin lingerie sleeves; a big bow of satin ribbon across the jacket held it securely in position over the bloused lace front with which the model I am describing was supplied.

The result is no licensed saloon will exist in the lower part of Westmoreland after May the 13th, except at the Mount Holly Hotel. Reported by Mr. Davis.


Fire originated in the big forest Friday last, near Mr. W. R. Gardy's mill, and after much effort on the part of the people residing in that section it was subdued; but on Saturday evening while the wind was blowing at a fearful rate from the south, it broke out with new fire, destroying everything in its wide path of a hundred or more acres of valuable young timber, until it reached the location of the big W. R. Gardy mill, where five thousand feet of rough and dressed lumber was turned into ashes. It was by extra effort the mill with all its machinery was saved. The loss and damage, which is estimated at nine hundred dollars, falls heavily on the young men, Messrs. Harvey & Co., who have recently purchased the entire business of Mr. Gardy. No insurance.


The earth is exceedingly dry and dusty and corn and other seeds remain in the ground, showing little signs of germination. Peas of the variety used for hay are scarce, and in great demand at 80 cents per bushel. Many of our farmers are preparing land to be planted as a crop for cultivation, to be picked and hulled. Thirty to thirty-five bushels can be afforded to the acre. Such a yield at the present price makes the crop far ahead of corn for profit. In addition, practical experience establishes the fact that land seeded in peas improves each year, also by their use in the soil all spurious grass and weeds are removed by this king of the soil.


Herring, shad and catfish are now being furnished by the Potomac trappers in abundance.


Mr. Robt. Anadale, a merchant at Baynesville, is the owner of a young beagle dog named George, that makes his rounds daily in the afternoon, in search of eggs among the bushes and brush adjacent to the store. George will handle them carefully and bring his findings to the store, walk proudly to the box where the store eggs are deposited and very cautiously lay down the egg, then go to the cracker barrel and whine, until his master, Mr. Anadale, gives him a cracker as a reward. Mr. Anadale values him at 500.

A. D. Stewart went to Kansas City Wednesday night.

Hon. Q. R. Bushaw, state senator, of Colby, was in Goodland Friday.

Mrs. A. G. Gulick left Thursday morning for short visit to relatives at Phillipsburg.

Mrs. H. Farrow celebrated her 61st birthday October 9. She is a native of Virginia and was married to the doctor in Harrison county, Kan., March 9, 1867.

Mrs. J. F. Stevens, Mrs. Wilhelmina Bradshaw and Mrs. Gregys, all of Wallace county, were in town Monday in attendance at the Eastern Star meeting and banquet.

Rev. John G. Anderson, dean of Salina, held divine services in the Episcopal mission Chapel Sunday both morning and evening. He is an excellent man and an interesting speaker.

Aaron Wells has bought the Whistler place and will move his barn from the Smoky to the Whistler place. He began operations Wednesday and was in town to get moving timbers.

F. N. Fox returned about the first of October from a month's trip in the mountains. He and Mrs. Fox went in a spring wagon for an outing. Mr. Fox has been afflicted with boils since his return and he lays it to bad alkali water.

H. Coleman, of Elliott, Ia., brother of Wesley Coleman, and Mrs. L. B. Miner, of Virginia, Ill., a widowed sister and brother here. The three have not met together for 40 years. Wesley Coleman is the youngest of the three.
